_comment: PG-001 Mode C drift-catch evaluation corpus. SYNTHETIC ONLY -- every name, number, address and clinical scenario below was invented for this file. No real patient data, no real person, no real record. Track A/Track B split, same as the Indic OCR corpus. Annotation guide and known biases: docs/pg001_mode_c_drift_detector.md section 6. Fields: id, category, clinical (is a real person's care being discussed), entities (personal-identifier spans; patient_linked marks whether the person is a patient or someone connected to one), why (why this segment is in the corpus).

text: Mrs Kalyani Devi in bed 14 is still febrile, start her on ceftriaxone one gram BD.
why: Baseline easy case: honorific-led name, cued bed number, unambiguous drug.

text: Patient MRN 4471029 was admitted last night with chest pain and troponin is rising.
why: Cue-led record number in obviously clinical narrative.

text: The 62-year-old male in cabin 3 had a myocardial infarction, we have started heparin.
why: Standard case-presentation opener; 'cabin' instead of 'bed' tests vocabulary breadth.

text: Can you pull up the discharge summary for UHID MH-2291043, the diabetic foot case?
why: Alphanumeric record number with a cue; also matches the bare-shape rule, so it tests overlap resolution.

text: Her DOB is 12/03/1961 and she is on metformin and insulin both.
why: Date only becomes an identifier because of the DOB cue.

text: Ward 7 attendant's number is 9845112233, call them about the consent form for surgery.
why: Attendant contact is patient-linked even though it is not the patient's own number.

text: Send the biopsy report to rekha.nair@example-hospital.test before the ward round.
why: Email belongs to a colleague, not a patient -- tests the patient_linked split.

text: Mr Iqbal Ahmed, 58/M, admitted in HDU with sepsis and hypotension.
why: Compressed 58/M form rather than the spelled-out age descriptor.

text: The child in bed 22B is spiking a temperature again, blood culture was sent yesterday.
why: Alphanumeric bed; patient referred to only by location, which is itself the identifier.

text: Aadhaar on the form is 4321 8765 2109 and the family lives at 14 Nehru Road, so follow-up is easy.
why: National ID and street address, the two highest-harm identifiers in this list.

text: Start broad-spectrum antibiotics and repeat the creatinine in the morning.
why: Clinical decision-making with nothing identifying at all. Identifier recall is undefined here; only the clinical-topic score matters.

text: The creatinine has doubled since admission, hold the metformin.
why: Two strong clinical terms, zero identifiers.

text: If the saturation drops below ninety again we should think about intubating.
why: 'intubating' is a morphological variant of a lexicon entry -- deliberately tests inflection handling.

text: Send blood culture and urine culture before the first dose goes in.
why: Ordering investigations; no patient reference of any kind.

text: There is a new murmur on examination, get an echocardiogram today.
why: 'murmur' is not in the lexicon; the case rests on 'echocardiogram' alone.

text: The HbA1c came back at nine point two, we need to restart insulin.
why: Lab value spoken as words, which STT commonly produces.

text: Post-op day two and there is still no bowel sound, keep him nil by mouth.
why: Ward-round shorthand.

text: The chest x-ray shows a right lower lobe consolidation, treat as pneumonia.
why: Imaging finding plus working diagnosis.

text: Taper the prednisolone over the next ten days and review in clinic.
why: Medication plan.

text: She is afebrile now but the leucocyte count is still climbing.
why: Pronoun-only patient reference; no identifier exists to be found.

text: Hold the heparin until the platelet count comes back.
why: Short utterance -- tests whether one or two strong terms are enough.

text: Get a repeat ECG if the chest pain comes back at all.
why: Abbreviation plus symptom phrase.

text: The chap in the corner bed is still bringing up everything he eats.
why: HARD. Real clinical content -- persistent vomiting in an inpatient -- with no clinical vocabulary and no numbered bed. Expected miss.

text: The old lady we saw this morning is not picking up, family wants to take her home.
why: HARD. A deteriorating patient and a discharge-against-advice conversation, phrased entirely in ordinary words. Expected miss.

text: He has gone downhill since the night shift, I think we should call the family in.
why: HARD. End-of-life conversation with zero lexicon hits. Expected miss.

text: The one who came in with the crush injury is going to theatre at two.
why: HARD. 'theatre' alone is not in the lexicon; only 'operation theatre' is. Deliberate near-miss.

text: Number four is asking for something for the pain again.
why: HARD. Bed referred to by bare ordinal; analgesia request phrased colloquially.

text: Sugars are all over the place since we changed the timing of her jab.
why: HARD. 'sugars' and 'jab' are the everyday forms of 'blood sugar' and 'insulin injection'; neither is in the lexicon.

text: Keep an eye on the drain output overnight and let me know if it is more than usual.
why: HARD. Post-operative nursing instruction in plain language.

text: She has been on the same drip since yesterday and nobody has reviewed it.
why: HARD. 'drip' alone rather than 'saline drip'.

text: Can you check whether the projector in the seminar room is booked for Friday?
why: Ordinary admin request.

text: Remind me to renew the car insurance before the end of the month.
why: Ordinary personal errand.

text: What is the weather looking like for the drive to Pune tomorrow?
why: Contains a capitalised place name mid-sentence -- a person-name false-positive trap.

text: Order two kilos of rice and some cooking oil from the usual shop.
why: Ordinary household request.

text: The wifi keeps dropping every time the microwave runs.
why: Ordinary complaint with a non-clinical context marker.

text: Play something instrumental, I need to concentrate on this spreadsheet.
why: Ordinary assistant command.

text: Book me a taxi to the airport at five in the morning.
why: Ordinary travel request.

text: How much did we spend on electricity last quarter?
why: Ordinary finance question.

text: Set an alarm for six and remind me about the gym.
why: Ordinary scheduling.

text: The printer in room 12 is jammed again, ask facilities to look at it.
why: A room number that identifies no one. Tests whether the bed/room rule is confidence-graded rather than binary.

text: The production database is in a critical state, we need to restore from backup.
why: HARD. 'critical' in its software sense.

text: That server has been unstable since the last deployment, keep an eye on it.
why: HARD. 'unstable' near a monitoring instruction.

text: We had to operate on the gearbox and the mechanic says it is a chronic problem.
why: HARD. 'operate' and 'chronic' in a mechanical sense.

text: My laptop caught a virus from that USB drive and the whole thing needs a clean install.
why: HARD. Disease metaphor applied to a computer.

text: The team is in recovery mode after the outage, treatment of the root cause comes next.
why: HARD. Two weak clinical words stacked in a project-management sentence.

text: Monitor the CPU temperature, it spikes whenever we compile the whole repository.
why: HARD. 'monitor' and 'spikes' in an engineering sense.

text: This spreadsheet is haemorrhaging money on line items nobody reviews.
why: HARD. A medical verb used financially.

text: The match was painful to watch, our openers are chronically out of form.
why: HARD. Inflected form of a lexicon entry in a sports context.

text: I need a diagnosis on why the build keeps failing on Windows only.
why: HARD. 'diagnosis' used about software; sits just under the default drift threshold, so it tests where the line falls.

text: Give the intern a dose of reality about deadlines before the appraisal.
why: HARD. 'dose' idiomatically.

text: Our flight is stable at thirty thousand feet and the turbulence has passed.
why: HARD. 'stable' in an aviation sense.

text: The plumber says the pressure in the pipes is too high and it is chronic in this building.
why: HARD. 'pressure' and 'chronic' in a plumbing sense.

text: Call Ramesh Iyer on 9812345678 about the flat's rent agreement.
why: Real identifiers, no patient. The detector cannot tell whose name this is -- only the policy engine's session context can.

text: Mail the invoice to arun.krishnan@example-vendor.test by Friday.
why: Vendor email in a plainly non-clinical sentence.

text: Mr Suresh Menon from the landlord's office is coming at four.
why: Honorific-led name with no clinical context at all.

text: My cousin lives at 22 Gandhi Street and we are meeting there for dinner.
why: Address belonging to a relative, not a patient.

text: Add Priya Sharma to the project channel and share the slide deck.
why: Colleague name in a workplace instruction.

text: The taxi driver's number is 987 654 3210 if the pickup is delayed.
why: Space-separated phone format.

text: Dr Fernandes is speaking at the conference on Thursday and is not seeing anyone.
why: A doctor's name in a non-clinical sentence -- 'Dr' is not evidence of clinical content.

text: My passport and Aadhaar 5566 7788 9900 both need updating on the portal.
why: The speaker's own national ID; sensitive, but not a patient identifier.

text: Book meeting room 4 for the vendor call with Anita Rao.
why: A room number that is not a bed, alongside a real name.

text: Ask Vikram to send the electricity bill for the Bengaluru office.
why: Single-token name plus a capitalised city -- one is a name, one is not.

text: Bed 9 and bed 11 need to swap, the family requested it.
why: Two identifiers, almost no clinical vocabulary. Borderline: ward logistics about named-by-location inpatients. Annotated clinical because the beds refer to specific people.

text: Get me the file for Sunita Bhosale, the one from Tuesday.
why: Genuinely borderline -- 'the file for X' is clinical only if X is a patient, which the text does not say. Annotated clinical; a different annotator could defensibly say otherwise.

text: UHID 8821004 needs the report faxed across.
why: Record number is the only clinical signal in the sentence.

text: Move him from 6 to 12 before the ward round.
why: Bed nouns elided entirely; only the surrounding clinical phrase makes the bare numbers interpretable.

text: Mrs Latha's husband called from 9900112233 asking about visiting hours.
why: Patient-linked contact detail with no clinical vocabulary.

text: Shift the 34-year-old female to the other side after lunch.
why: Age-sex descriptor carrying the whole patient reference.

text: My mother's blood sugar was 240 this morning and she skipped her metformin.
why: CONTESTED. A family member's health, not a hospital patient. Annotated clinical because it is a named person's health data crossing a remote link; a deployment could reasonably classify it differently, and that ambiguity is the point.

text: The textbook case is a 45-year-old male with dyspnoea and a raised JVP, purely for the exam.
why: HARD FALSE POSITIVE. Dense clinical language about a person who does not exist. No real identifier, so the age-sex span is deliberately not annotated -- a detector hit there is a true false positive.

text: I am reading a novel where the surgeon poisons a patient with insulin.
why: HARD FALSE POSITIVE. Fiction. Three strong lexicon terms, zero real clinical content.

text: The medical drama we watched had a whole episode about sepsis and antibiotics.
why: HARD FALSE POSITIVE. Television, not care.

text: Regarding the gentleman we discussed, the plan stands and I will see him tomorrow.
why: HARD FALSE NEGATIVE. Deliberately vague clinical follow-up -- exactly what a physician says when they are being discreet, and exactly what a lexicon cannot catch.

text: the patient in bed 4 is septic, start meropenem now
why: Lowercase, unpunctuated -- what raw STT output actually looks like. Tests whether case-dependent rules degrade. 'meropenem' is intentionally absent from the lexicon.

text: kalyani devi in bed 14 is still febrile
why: The co-01 sentence with STT-realistic lowercasing. Structural name detection depends on capitalisation, so this is an expected and important miss.
